summary: Specifies a mapping between X.400 (1988) / ISO 10021 mail and the Internet mail format of RFC 822, for use on the DARPA Internet and in the UK Academic Community. It was replaced by RFC 2156.

eli5.summary: Two kinds of email systems spoke different languages. This document is a translation guide so a message from one can be understood by the other.

questions: convert x.400 mail to internet mail
what is an x.400 to rfc 822 gateway
how are x.400 addresses mapped to internet email
subtitle: A translation guide that lets X.400 mail systems and RFC 822 Internet mail exchange messages through a gateway.

tldr.problem: Two incompatible mail worlds existed: X.400 (1988) / ISO 10021 message handling and the RFC 822 mail used on the DARPA Internet, UUCP, Bitnet and JNT Mail networks. Users on each side wanted to reach the other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines detailed mappings, in both directions, between RFC 822 messages and X.400 interpersonal messages, including how to translate addresses, headers, reports and notifications, so that gateways behave consistently.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1327 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFCs 987, 1026, 1138 and 1148. It was itself obsoleted by RFC 2156 and updated by RFC 1495.

today: RFC 1327 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2156 and updated by RFC 1495. It obsoleted RFCs 987, 1026, 1138 and 1148 and is marked as updating RFC 822.

sections.title: Why Mail Needs a Gateway
sections.content:
RFC 1327 describes a set of mappings that enable interworking between systems running the CCITT X.400 (1988) Recommendations, also known as ISO/IEC 10021 or MOTIS, and systems using the RFC 822 mail protocol or protocols derived from it. The approach aims to maximise the services offered across the boundary without requiring unduly complex mappings. It should not require any change to end systems.

On the RFC 822 side the document covers several kinds of network: SMTP networks (RFC 821 plus RFC 920 domains), UUCP networks, parts of Bitnet, and JNT Mail (Greybook) networks used by the UK Academic Community. The specification is meant to be used when this mapping is performed on the DARPA Internet or in the UK Academic Community.

The RFC lists five guiding principles, which it calls goals rather than guarantees: be pragmatic, keep functionality across the gateway as high as possible, avoid losing information, remember that a gateway must understand the semantics one level above the layer it works on, and keep the mapping reversible where possible. It also warns that the rest of the text is technically dense and assumes you already know RFC 822 and X.400 (1988).
sections.eli5: People using two different kinds of email want to write to each other. The gateway translates carefully, tries not to lose any part of the message, and tries to make sure the translation can be undone.

sections.title: The Gatewaying Model
sections.content:
X.400 defines an Interpersonal Messaging System (IPMS) on top of a store-and-forward Message Transfer System. Its main objects are the IPM (Interpersonal Message, made of a heading and a body of one or more body parts), the IPN (Interpersonal Notification about receipt), probes, and delivery reports. RFC 822 assumes an underlying "822-MTS" service that identifies a list of recipients, identifies an error return address and transfers an RFC 822 message, which consists of a header and uninterpreted ASCII text.

The gateway does not map these cleanly layer to layer. The RFC says reality does not fit the elegant approaches and describes a "slightly tangled" mapping. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, a message plus its 822-MTS information is always mapped into an IPM. Going from X.400 to RFC 822, the result can be derived from a report, an IPN or an IPM. Probes must be processed by the gateway, and messages whose content type is not defined by the IPMS are not mapped and should be rejected.

Chapter 2 rates each service as Supported, Not Supported or Partial Support. A service counts as supported only if there is semantic correspondence, no significant loss of information and any required actions are taken. Where the standard has no equivalent, the RFC often carries the information in an extension, such as a new "RFC 822 Header Field" service on the X.400 side. Repeated trips through gateways are supported but tend toward the lowest common denominator, roughly the services of RFC 822.
sections.eli5: The translator knows what a letter, a receipt and a bounced-mail note look like in both languages. When one language has no word for something, the translator tucks the original words into a margin note so nothing is thrown away.

sections.title: Basic Mappings Between Text and ASN.1
sections.content:
X.400 is encoded with ASN.1, while RFC 822 is text. Chapter 3 defines a notation and conversions for common types. A gateway interprets all IA5 as ASCII. Booleans become TRUE or FALSE. Time values map between UTCTime and the RFC 822 date-time syntax, with the timezone preserved as given and the date never normalised to another timezone. If a date cannot be parsed, the RFC recommends using the time of translation.

Some strings in X.400 are PrintableString, which lacks characters such as @, %, !, " and _ that are common in RFC 822 addresses. The RFC therefore defines escapes: (a) for at sign, (p) for percent, (b) for exclamation mark, (q) for double quote, (u) for underscore, (l) and (r) for round brackets, and ( followed by three decimal digits and ) for any other ASCII character. Teletex strings use a similar quoting of the form { followed by three-digit octets and }.
sections.eli5: Some of the letters and symbols that email addresses use are not allowed in the other system. So the translator spells them out with secret codes, like writing "(a)" every time it means the at sign.

sections.title: Addressing
sections.content:
The RFC calls addressing probably the trickiest problem of the gateway. An X.400 O/R Address (MTS.ORAddress) is a set of attribute and value pairs, such as country (C), administration domain (ADMD), private domain (PRMD), organization (O), organizational units (OU), personal name (PN) and domain defined attributes (DD). The RFC gives each attribute a key and a text encoding so the whole address can be written in ASCII, and requires that all components are encoded so that error messages can be returned.

In the standard textual form each pair is written as /key=value/, and the characters / and = are quoted with $. Personal names get a friendlier form: a given name of Marshall and surname Rose map to Marshall.Rose, and initials MT with surname Rose map to M.T.Rose. An RFC 822 address that has no X.400 equivalent can be carried inside a domain defined attribute named RFC-822.

The mapping between the two address styles is deliberately asymmetrical. The RFC gives two reasons: the syntaxes are too different, and in general there is not the administrative cooperation between the X.400 and RFC 822 worlds that a symmetrical global mapping would need. Gateways therefore rely on mapping tables, whose format is given in Appendix F.
sections.eli5: An address in one system looks like a street address, and in the other like a phone number. The translator has a lookup book and a set of spelling rules so a letter still finds the right house on the other side.

sections.title: Detailed Mappings in Each Direction
sections.content:
From RFC 822 to X.400, one IP Message is generated per message. The headers become the IPMS heading and the message body becomes a single IA5 body part. The mappings include From: to the originator (or to the authorizing users if a Sender: is present), To: to primary recipients, Cc: to copy recipients, Subject: to the subject, and Message-Id: to the IPM identifier. A Comments: field becomes its own body part placed first. Fields with no standard slot, such as Keywords:, Encrypted:, Resent-* and X-* fields, travel in a new heading extension called rfc-822-field, so nothing is dropped.

The generated IPM uses content type 2, or content type 22 when 1988 features such as the extension are used. Because X.400 has upper bounds on field sizes, the RFC allows three options, all conforming: ignore the bounds, reject the message, or truncate fields.

From X.400 to RFC 822, a single RFC 822 message is built from an IP Message, a report or an IPN. All body parts become one RFC 822 body, and other services become header fields, with new fields defined where none exists. If the mapping does not produce one, the gateway supplies defaults: an 822-MTS originator pointing at a gateway administrator, a Date: field, a From: field, and, if there is no recipient field, To: list:;.
sections.eli5: Going one way, the translator puts the plain letter in an official envelope and tapes any odd extra notes inside. Going back, it unpacks the envelope into a plain letter and makes sure it has a date, a sender and a to line, even if it has to fill them in.

sections.title: Older X.400, Extensions and Conformance
sections.content:
The mapping targets the full 1988 version of X.400, not a 1984 subset. Appendix G explains how to interwork with X.400(1984): when mapping from 1984 to RFC 822 no changes are needed, but when mapping to 1984 the extension headers are instead placed in the first IA5 body part, which starts with the line RFC-822-Headers:. This follows the older RFC 987 approach.

Appendix H defines optional RFC 822 headers that give access to some X.400 services, including Prevent-NonDelivery-Report, Generate-Delivery-Report, Alternate-Recipient, Disclose-Recipients and Content-Return. Appendix I states that conformance cannot be claimed unless all mandatory features are implemented, including the formats of all fields, subject lines, delivery reports and IPNs, all mappings of trace information, and a mechanism to reach all three global mappings. A gateway should state which 822-MTS protocols it supports (SMTP, JNT Mail, UUCP), which X.400 versions it supports, and how it handles upper bounds and unconvertible body parts. Subsetting the specification is strongly discouraged.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: The rulebook says how to handle older versions of the other language, offers some optional shortcuts, and lists what a translator must do to be called a proper one. It does not say anything about keeping messages secret.
